He contrasts his vision with the approaches of Zola and Dickens, and uses a concrete example of everyday love-making he witnessed to illustrate his commitment to depicting "the ignobly decent" without editorial commentary or artificial effect.

She proposes that he retreat to the seaside alone to recover his health and write a successful book while she and their child stay with her mother. Reardon expresses dread at their separation and hints at self-destruction if his efforts fail. Amy responds emotionally, insisting on her love. This quoted line comes from Reardon's response to Amy's tearful plea, as he agrees to pursue her plan despite his despair.
c15:p102: After an emotional confrontation where Reardon accuses Amy of abandoning him during his financial troubles, Amy returns to him late at night in tears. She confesses her love and proposes that he separate temporarily to recover his health and write a successful book while she stays with her mother. Following an intimate reconciliation where Reardon asks for repeated reassurance of her love, this moment captures Amy's exhausted silence as they embrace in the cold study at three in the morning, before she suggests they retire to bed.
c15:p103: This line is spoken by Amy to Edwin Reardon in the early morning hours after they have reconciled following a bitter quarrel. Amy has come to his study at 3 AM, finding him in despair, and they have embraced passionately. She is now urging him to leave the cold study and come to bed with her, marking a moment of renewed intimacy and her renewed commitment to supporting his literary ambitions through a plan to separate temporarily so he can recover his health and write a successful book away from financial worries.
c15:p104: Edwin and Amy reconcile after a bitter quarrel about her supposed coldness during his financial struggles. After hours of passionate conversation in which Amy convinces him to attempt one final effort to restore their fortunes by taking a solitary retreat to the seaside to write, they embrace intimately. As dawn approaches and the clock strikes three, Amy urges them to leave the cold study and retire to bed.
c15:p105: After a painful marital confrontation in which Reardon accuses Amy of abandoning him during his financial struggles, Amy reconciles with him late at night and proposes a plan: Reardon should rent out their flat, retreat to the seaside to recover his health and write a successful book while she and their son stay with her mother. The next day, buoyed by this new hope and Amy's renewed affection, they walk together and encounter wealthy people, prompting Reardon's bitter reflections on the transformative power of money and the degrading effects of poverty.
c15:p106: Edwin Reardon, impoverished and struggling as a writer, observes wealthy people passing by during a walk with his wife Amy. He reflects bitterly on the vast gulf between rich and poor, expressing his sense of deprivation and the seemingly insurmountable distance between their social worlds.
c15:p107: Edwin Reardon and Amy discuss the vast difference between the wealthy and the poor during their afternoon walk. Amy sighs in agreement when Reardon laments how the rich possess powers and freedoms that seem supernatural to those in poverty, unable to gratify their desires or enjoy luxurious homes as the wealthy do.
c15:p108: Reardon and Amy take a walk together and observe wealthy people in carriages and luxurious houses. Reardon becomes absorbed in envious contemplation of wealth, imagining what it would be like to wake each morning with all desires gratified and to live in such opulent surroundings, contrasting sharply with his own impoverished circumstances.
c15:p109: Edwin Reardon and Amy are walking together and observe wealthy people in an open carriage and on horseback. Reardon envies their wealth and the freedom it provides, marveling at how money transforms every detail of life. Amy responds to his extended meditation on the vast difference between rich and poor with this dismissive comment about the wealthy, suggesting their material advantages don't reflect any superior qualities.
c15:p110: Reardon and Amy take a walk together and encounter an open carriage with wealthy people. This prompts Reardon to deliver an extended meditation on the transformative power of wealth and the degrading effects of poverty. He argues that money fundamentally alters every aspect of life, comparing the difference between rich and poor to that between a whole man and a maimed one. He expresses envy of the rich while acknowledging their inability to fully appreciate their own happiness.
c15:p111: Edwin Reardon and Amy are taking a walk together after reconciling from a quarrel. During their conversation, Reardon begins dwelling on the vast difference between the wealthy and the poor, expressing envious thoughts about the luxuries of rich people and lamenting how poverty constrains his life and creative abilities. Amy becomes troubled by his obsessive focus on this depressing subject, which undermines the hopeful mood she has been trying to maintain about his planned retreat to the countryside to write a successful new book.
c15:p112: Edwin Reardon and Amy are on an afternoon walk together, discussing their financial desperation. Reardon reflects on the profound psychological and physiological differences between the wealthy and the poor, arguing that poverty fundamentally degrades the mind and brain itself, leaving no thought untainted by the struggle for survival.
c15:p113: Amy and Reardon are walking together and discussing the psychological and physiological effects of poverty. Reardon has been reflecting on how poverty affects the human mind and brain, comparing it to slavery. Amy responds by elaborating on how poverty pervades every mental function rather than being a localized suffering, coloring all of one's thoughts and experiences.
c15:p114: This passage occurs during an afternoon walk between Edwin Reardon and Amy following their reconciliation the previous night. Reardon has been expounding on the differences between wealth and poverty, comparing the lives of the rich to those of the poor. Amy has just acknowledged that poverty has affected her negatively, and Reardon responds with this philosophical meditation on how poverty permeates every aspect of human experience, drawing a parallel between modern poverty and ancient slavery.
c15:p115: Amy and Reardon are walking together discussing the debilitating effects of poverty on their lives and prospects. Reardon has been expounding on how poverty pervades every aspect of human experience, comparing it to slavery. Amy interrupts with this confession, acknowledging that their financial struggles have negatively affected her own character and emotional state.
c15:p116: Edwin Reardon and his wife Amy are walking together discussing the stark difference between their impoverished life and the wealth of the rich. Amy mentions that poverty affects every function of the brain and colors every thought. Reardon agrees, comparing poverty to slavery. c15:p120: Edwin Reardon opens a copy of his newly published novel "Margaret Home" and, distressed by the poor quality of his own writing, laments the suffering he endured while composing it and expresses despair over how readers will never appreciate the author's struggle behind even flawed prose.
c15:p121: Edwin Reardon receives the published copies of his novel "Margaret Home" and discusses with his wife Amy which people should receive complimentary copies of the book.
c15:p122: Edwin Reardon has just received the published copies of his novel "Margaret Home." When asked who should receive copies, he expresses reluctance to distribute them, suggesting most copies should be burned for kindling, but acknowledges his mother-in-law will likely expect one.
c15:p123: Edwin Reardon has just received published copies of his book "Margaret Home" and is deciding which people should receive copies. When Amy asks if Milvain should get one, Edwin responds with reluctant indifference, acknowledging that Milvain will likely expect a copy.
c15:p124: Edwin Reardon discusses with Amy which people should receive complimentary copies of his newly published novel "Margaret Home." c15:p126: Edwin Reardon dismisses Amy's request to give a copy of his newly published book "Margaret Home" to Mrs. Carter, showing his indifference to the book's fate.
c15:p127: Edwin Reardon receives published copies of his new book "Margaret Home" and places it on his shelf of previous works while Amy watches, a moment reflecting their diminished circumstances and his anxieties about the book's success.
c15:p128: Amy gazes at Edwin's published books arranged on a shelf and remarks on his collected works, a moment that prompts Edwin to lament how his creative powers have declined since writing his earlier masterpiece "On Neutral Ground," contrasting his past productive energy with his current struggle to write under financial pressure.
c15:p129: Edwin Reardon examines his newly published book "Margaret Home" and despairs over its quality, comparing his current creative decline to his earlier success with "On Neutral Ground." c15:p130: Amy encourages Reardon after he expresses despair about his declining literary abilities, comparing his former creative powers to his current struggles. c15:p131: Edwin Reardon reflects on his creative process while writing his earlier successful novel "On Neutral Ground," contrasting his past productive workflow and inspired state with his current struggles. c15:p132: Amy reassures Reardon that his creative powers will return after he recovers his health, following his nostalgic reminiscence about the ease and inspiration he experienced while writing his earlier novel "On Neutral Ground."
c15:p133: Edwin Reardon is reflecting on the contrast between his earlier writing life and his current dire financial circumstances. c15:p134: Edwin Reardon reflects on his lost creative powers after publishing "Margaret Home," wishing he could encounter a wealthy patron to help him earn a modest income so he could write without financial desperation.
c15:p135: Edwin Reardon reflects on his financial desperation while contemplating his published works. After viewing his books on a shelf, he fantasizes about a wealthy patron discovering his talent and providing financial support to help him escape poverty.

c15:p137: Edwin Reardon laments his financial desperation and wishes for patronage like Coleridge received from Gillman. He expresses that he doesn't need to be housed, only enough income to escape poverty and have time for writing without constant anxiety about the workhouse.
c15:p138: Edwin Reardon, struggling with poverty and literary failure, expresses despair about their financial situation and wistfully imagines encountering a wealthy patron who might help him earn a modest income. c15:p139: Edwin Reardon has just received the published copies of his novel "Margaret Home" and despairingly critiqued its quality to Amy. c15:p141: Milvain visits Reardon and Amy to obtain a copy of Reardon's newly published novel "Margaret Home." Reardon responds with reluctance and indifference when Milvain requests his author's copy, revealing his pessimism about the book's quality and reception.
c15:p142: Milvain visits Reardon to obtain a copy of his newly published novel "Margaret Home." Milvain mentions he has already read it from the library, anticipating that Reardon would not send him a copy, as he wants to collect all of Reardon's works.

c15:p144: Milvain visits Reardon late one evening to obtain a copy of his newly published novel "Margaret Home." c15:p145: Milvain is discussing Reardon's newly published novel "Margaret Home," arguing that while the three-volume format forced Reardon to expand the story unnecessarily, the underlying motive or plot of the book is adequate, though poorly executed.
c15:p146: Milvain visits Reardon and praises his newly published book "Margaret Home," suggesting it could succeed if condensed to one volume. Reardon dismissively counters that the motive is merely adequate, only serving to highlight the poor execution of the work.
c15:p147: Milvain visits Reardon to collect a copy of his newly published novel "Margaret Home." After Reardon dismissively comments on the book's poor quality, Milvain defends it and begins discussing the structural problems caused by the three-volume novel format that publishers forced authors to use.
c15:p148: Milvain criticizes the three-volume novel system as exploitative of English novelists while visiting Reardon. c15:p149: Reardon defends the three-volume novel format to Milvain, explaining that authors of moderate reputation depend on the higher payment for three-volume novels and the circulating libraries' support to earn a livelihood. c15:p150: Milvain and Reardon discuss the commercial constraints of Victorian publishing. Milvain argues that circulating libraries should distribute single-volume novels instead of the standard three-volume format, to which Reardon replies with this statement about the lack of practical barriers to such a change, though he notes it would reduce library profits.
c15:p151: A discussion between Reardon and Milvain about the publishing industry's economic structure, specifically regarding why circulating libraries prefer three-volume novels over single-volume ones. c15:p152: Milvain visits Reardon to discuss his newly published book "Margaret Home." c15:p153: Reardon tells Milvain that his one-volume novel is nearly completed when asked about it during Milvain's brief evening visit.
c15:p154: Milvain advises Reardon to personally submit his nearly completed one-volume novel to the publisher Jedwood, suggesting he is approachable and fair-minded, during a brief evening visit where they discuss the commercial difficulties of the three-volume novel system and Reardon's struggling literary career.

c15:p161: Edwin Reardon and his wife Amy have agreed to a separation plan to save their marriage and finances: Reardon will rent out their flat, move to the seaside resort town of Worthing to live cheaply and write a new book, while Amy stays with her mother. c15:p162: Edwin Reardon and his wife Amy discuss their plan for him to leave London and retreat to the seaside town of Worthing to recover his health and write a successful book, while Amy and their son stay with her mother. c15:p163: Amy reassures Reardon that her eagerness to separate temporarily—by having him go to the seaside to recover his health and write—is motivated solely by concern for his welfare, not by a desire to abandon him.
c15:p164: Edwin Reardon expresses doubt about his ability to sell his completed manuscript, questioning the viability of the plan he and Amy have devised to separate temporarily while he attempts to write a successful book at the seaside in order to escape their worsening poverty.
c15:p165: Amy reassures Reardon about his financial prospects as they plan his separation. c15:p166: Edwin Reardon expresses doubt about his ability to work productively if he cannot sell his completed book. c15:p167: Amy encourages Reardon about his plan to separate temporarily, rent out their flat, and retreat to the seaside (Worthing) to write a new book. c15:p168: Edwin Reardon and his wife Amy have agreed to a separation plan to save their marriage and finances. c15:p169: Edwin Reardon plans to retreat to Worthing to write a new book while his wife Amy and child live with her mother. c15:p170: Edwin Reardon, a struggling writer suffering from poverty and mental exhaustion, has reconciled with his wife Amy after a bitter quarrel. c16:p0: This passage opens the chapter and introduces Reardon's psychological state regarding critical reception of his novel 'Margaret Home.' c16:p1: This passage reveals Reardon's defensive psychological state regarding critical reception of his novel "Margaret Home." c17:p110: During an intense confrontation with his wife Amy, Reardon passionately defends his decision to take a clerk position rather than continue pursuing literary success. c17:p111: Reardon has just accepted a clerk position at a hospital to support his family, rejecting his plan to retreat to the seaside and focus on writing. c17:p112: Amy and Reardon have been arguing intensely about his decision to accept a clerkship. c17:p113: Amy challenges Reardon to prove her wrong about his decision to become a clerk at the hospital. c17:p115: Amy challenges Reardon to prove he is willing to prevent their descent into poverty and social disgrace by refusing to take a clerk position, insisting instead that he continue pursuing literary success rather than accept what she views as a degrading occupation.
c17:p116: Reardon defends himself during a heated argument with Amy about taking a clerkship position. c17:p119: In this scene, Amy has just refused Reardon's plan to take a clerk position and live in cheaper rooms in Islington. c17:p120: Amy demands that Reardon immediately go to Mr. Carter and retract his acceptance of the clerk position, which she considers a disgraceful comedown. c17:p121: Reardon rejects Amy's demand that he renounce the clerkship position he has just accepted from Mr. Carter. c17:p122: Amy attempts to persuade Reardon to reject the clerical position he has just accepted from Carter, commanding him to rescind his offer immediately. c17:p123: Reardon refuses Amy's demand that he immediately tell Mr. Carter he cannot accept the clerk position, insisting instead on taking the job despite her shame at his social degradation.
c17:p124: Amy pleads with Reardon to reject the clerkship position he has accepted from Carter, offering to provide financial support herself and maintain social appearances while he focuses on writing another novel to restore their fortunes.
c17:p125: Amy demands that Reardon immediately go to Mr Carter and retract his acceptance of the clerk position, insisting that Carter must not spread news of this "disgrace" before Reardon can recant his decision. c17:p126: Reardon has just accepted a clerkship position with Carter to supplement his failed literary career. Amy refuses to accept this decision, viewing it as a shameful fall in social status. c17:p127: Amy refuses to accept Reardon's plan to become a hospital clerk, viewing it as a degrading fall in social status. c17:p128: Reardon defends his decision to accept a clerkship position by reminding Amy that he has worked as a clerk before, arguing that taking the position should not be considered a disgrace. c17:p129: Amy refuses to accept Reardon's decision to take a clerk position at twenty-five shillings a week, arguing that it constitutes a degrading fall from his current social status. c17:p130: Reardon confronts Amy about her refusal to live with him if he takes a clerk position. Amy argues that becoming a clerk would be a disgrace to her social standing, prompting Reardon to challenge her claim that they share the same world and values.
c17:p131: Amy pressures Reardon to retract his decision to become a clerk at the hospital, viewing it as a shameful degradation. c17:p132: After a heated argument about Reardon's decision to take a clerk's position at the hospital, Amy demands he go immediately to Mr. Carter and renounce the post, offering to find money herself to support him instead. c17:p133: Reardon has just accepted a clerkship position at a hospital to support his family, rejecting his wife Amy's plea that he abandon this decision. c17:p134: Amy has refused to accompany Reardon to modest lodgings in Islington, insisting instead that he reject the clerk position Carter offered him and continue pursuing literature. c17:p135: Amy's final declaration of separation from Reardon after he refuses to recant his decision to take a clerk position at the hospital, rejecting her demand that he abandon the post to preserve appearances and her social standing.
c17:p136: After their heated argument over Reardon's decision to accept a clerk position at the hospital rather than continue struggling as a writer, Amy demands he immediately rescind the job offer to preserve their social standing. c17:p137: After Reardon and Amy have a bitter quarrel about his decision to take a clerk's position at the hospital instead of continuing to pursue literary success, Amy refuses to live with him and demands he rescind the job offer. c17:p138: After a sleepless night following their bitter quarrel over Reardon's decision to take a clerk's position, the couple maintains a facade of normalcy during breakfast before Reardon prepares to leave and search for new lodgings in a poorer neighborhood.
c17:p139: After Amy leaves Reardon in the study following their bitter argument about his decision to take a clerk's position, they pass the night apart. c17:p140: Reardon tells Amy he is leaving to search for cheaper lodgings in Islington after accepting a clerk position at a hospital, which Amy refuses to accept as she considers it beneath their social station. She has decided to leave him and go to her mother's house with their child.

c17:p142: After Reardon decides to take a clerk position at a hospital rather than continue pursuing literary work, Amy refuses to live with him in cheaper lodgings and prepares to leave him. c17:p143: After their bitter quarrel about Reardon taking a clerk position, Amy has decided to leave him immediately rather than waiting until Tuesday. As she prepares to depart with their child, Reardon asks about dismissing their servant Lizzie.
c17:p144: Reardon, having decided to take a clerk position at a hospital despite Amy's opposition, instructs her to dismiss their servant Lizzie and pay her wages as he prepares to leave and find new lodgings. c17:p145: Reardon offers Amy money to dismiss the servant, but Amy insists on handling the dismissal herself, leading to their final goodbye as she prepares to leave him.
c17:p146: Reardon, having decided to take a clerkship despite Amy's opposition, prepares to leave the house to search for lodgings in Islington. c17:p147: Amy and Reardon have reached a breaking point in their marriage. c17:p148: Reardon's final farewell to Amy. c17:p149: Reardon has decided to take a clerk position despite Amy's strong opposition to this perceived degradation. After a night of separation, they meet for a final goodbye in the study. c17:p150: Reardon has just announced his decision to take a clerk position at a hospital, rejecting Amy's pleas to reconsider. c17:p151: Amy refuses to accompany Reardon to his new lodgings in Islington, declining to live with him as a clerk's wife despite his ultimatum that she must choose between following him or parting forever.
c17:p152: After their separation is finalized, Reardon tells Amy that if she refuses to join him in his new lodgings in Islington—accepting his decision to take a clerk position rather than continue pursuing literature—then she has chosen to leave him. c17:p153: Reardon leaves his wife Amy after their final confrontation over his decision to take a clerkship. c17:p154: After Reardon accepts a clerk position at a hospital despite Amy's strong objections, the couple has a final confrontation where Amy refuses to accompany him to his new lodgings in Islington. c17:p157: Reardon, after Amy has left him to stay with her mother, spends the evening packing his few possessions for his move to cheaper lodgings in Islington. c18:p0: This is the opening paragraph introducing Mrs Edmund Yule's character and background. It establishes her formative experiences of financial hardship as one of seven motherless sisters, explains how poverty shaped her contradictory nature—generous in impulse but stingy in practice—and sets up her widowhood as a period of declined circumstances that have made her pretentious and querulous. This character sketch forms the foundation for understanding her later behavior throughout the chapter, including her social ambitions, her treatment of servants and tradespeople, and her anxious response to her daughter Amy's marital crisis.
c18:p1: This passage describes Mrs. Edmund Yule's financial struggles and moral compromises. Having been widowed with limited means, she maintains an appearance of gentility by renting an expensive house in London while treating her servants and tradespeople poorly to cover her expenses. Though aware of her shameful behavior toward those she employs, she justifies her meanness as a necessary survival strategy in a harsh economic battle where she must either dominate others or be dominated herself.
c18:p2: This passage illustrates Mrs. Edmund Yule's contradictory moral character: she is genuinely moved by tales of poverty and injustice, yet her own financial constraints force her to behave meanly toward those she employs, such as underpaying her charwoman. The chunk exemplifies the central tension in her personality—between her natural compassion and the harsh economic realities that compel her to prioritize her own precarious social position over the welfare of others.
c18:p3: This passage occurs early in the chapter (paragraph 3) and provides crucial characterization of Mrs. Edmund Yule's contradictory nature: while ruthlessly mercenary toward servants and tradespeople, she is tenderly devoted to her children, particularly her daughter Amy. The narrator explains how Mrs. Yule carefully conceals her financial desperation and shameful behavior from Amy through strategic deception, while her son John has glimpsed the reality behind her genteel facade. This characterization becomes essential to understanding Mrs. Yule's later anxious reaction to Amy's marital separation and her obsession with maintaining social appearances despite financial strain.
c18:p4: This passage describes Mrs Edmund Yule's social aspirations and character. Rather than seeking to rise above her own social class, she focuses on maintaining superiority and respect within her limited circle of acquaintances. She is concerned with her reputation and how her name sounds to others, wanting to be perceived as a woman of refined taste and distinction. This characterization follows the earlier depiction of her financial struggles and moral compromises, and precedes the introduction of her daughter Amy's marriage to the novelist Edwin Reardon.
c18:p5: This chunk introduces Edwin Reardon as Amy's suitor, marking a pivotal moment in Mrs. Yule's hopes for her daughter's advantageous marriage. It establishes Mrs. Yule's high expectations for Amy—rejecting ordinary matches in favor of a husband of distinction—and Reardon's initial appearance as a promising literary figure who seems to fulfill these ambitions, before the chapter reveals his subsequent failure and the deterioration of Amy's marriage.
c18:p6: Mrs. Yule's initial reaction to learning that Amy's suitor, Edwin Reardon, is a novelist. She considers this a respectable form of distinction and hopes it will elevate Amy's social position, before later discovering his career disappoints her expectations.
c18:p7: This chunk occurs in paragraph P7, during Mrs. Yule's initial assessment of Edwin Reardon as a suitable husband for her daughter Amy. It represents Mrs. Yule's hopeful expectations that Reardon, though not physically vigorous, will achieve literary distinction and social prestige as a celebrated novelist, which would satisfy her desire for a son-in-law of intellectual standing. These optimistic anticipations directly precede the chapter's exploration of how those hopes are subsequently disappointed.
c18:p8: Mrs. Yule had hoped that Amy's marriage to novelist Edwin Reardon would elevate the family's social standing, envisioning him as a man of distinguished literary talent who would be welcomed in cultured circles. This sentence marks the turning point where those hopeful expectations begin to collapse as Reardon's career and social prospects deteriorate.
c18:p9: This passage depicts Mrs. Yule's social manipulation and damage control following Edwin Reardon's failure as a novelist. After initially welcoming him as a son-in-law of distinction, Mrs. Yule begins systematically distancing herself from him once his literary career falters and he becomes an embarrassment to her social pretensions. The chunk shows her spreading subtle rumors about his eccentricity to her social circle while privately grieving over Amy's disastrous marriage, all motivated by her obsession with maintaining respectability and controlling how others perceive her family.
c18:p10: This passage reflects Mrs. Yule's distress upon discovering that Amy has returned home separated from her husband Edwin Reardon, a novelist whose literary ambitions and financial prospects have collapsed. The chunk captures Mrs. Yule's primary concern: managing appearances and controlling the social narrative around Amy's marital separation, rather than addressing the actual crisis itself. It marks the moment of catastrophic revelation that transforms Mrs. Yule's earlier optimism about Amy's advantageous marriage into desperate anxiety about reputation damage.
c18:p11: Amy has unexpectedly returned to her mother's house with her child and belongings, having separated from her husband Edwin Reardon, a struggling novelist who has taken a clerical position earning only twenty-five shillings a week and expects her to live in poverty-stricken lodgings.
c18:p12: Amy has unexpectedly returned to her mother's house with her child and belongings, having separated from her husband Edwin Reardon due to his financial failure and inability to support her. Mrs Yule, observing the arrival from the window, learns that Amy has left her marriage.
c18:p13: Mrs. Yule learns from Amy that her husband Edwin Reardon has permanently left her, returning to their home with their child and belongings after he took a low-paying clerk position. Mrs. Yule's social reputation is devastated by this separation, as she must now explain Amy's return to society without revealing the shameful truth of their financial collapse.
c18:p14: Mrs. Yule has just learned that Amy has returned home with her child and belongings after separating from her husband Edwin Reardon, a struggling novelist who has taken a clerk's position at low wages. Amy's mother bursts into tears, calling the situation "disgraceful," but Amy responds with this line, indicating she has accepted the worst outcome and refuses to be consoled by her mother's emotional reaction.
c18:p15: Mrs Yule has just learned that her daughter Amy has returned to her mother's house with her child and belongings, having separated from her husband Edwin Reardon. Mrs Yule is devastated by this scandal, fearing how it will appear to her social circle and worrying about how to explain Amy's presence to friends and neighbors. She is shocked that Reardon has taken a clerk position earning only twenty-five shillings a week and expects Amy to live in poverty with him, which Amy has refused to do.
c18:p16: Amy responds defensively to her mother's concerns about explaining her separation from her husband Edwin Reardon to society. She insists on maintaining privacy about the scandal rather than offering explanations to acquaintances.
c18:p17: Mrs. Yule attempts to convince Amy that her husband Edwin Reardon is mentally unstable, suggesting this as an explanation for his decision to work as a clerk for meager wages instead of continuing his literary career. Mrs. Yule proposes spreading rumors of his mental derangement to account for Amy's sudden return to her mother's house.
c18:p18: Amy defends her husband Edwin Reardon against her mother's suggestion that he is mentally unstable, insisting he is of sound mind despite his financial failure and refusal to continue living beyond their means.
c18:p19: Mrs. Yule, upon learning that Amy has separated from her husband Edwin Reardon and returned home, attempts to convince Amy to let her spread rumors that Reardon is mentally unstable or "odd in his ways" to provide a socially acceptable explanation for the separation. c18:p20: Amy refuses her mother's suggestion to spread rumors about her husband Edwin Reardon being mentally unbalanced as an excuse for their separation. c18:p21: Mrs. Yule suggests to Amy that she should allow rumors of Reardon's mental instability to circulate as an explanation for their separation, arguing that Amy has already done her duty by him and that such rumors would provide social cover for her abandonment of her husband.
c18:p22: Amy refuses her mother's suggestion to spread rumors about Edwin Reardon's mental instability as an explanation for their separation, insisting it would be wrong to start such gossip despite Mrs. Yule's conviction that this falsehood would help manage their social reputation.
c18:p23: Amy has just returned home to her mother after separating from her husband Edwin Reardon, who has taken a clerk position earning minimal wages. Mrs. Yule suggests spreading rumors that Reardon is mentally unstable to explain Amy's departure to society. Amy weakly objects to this deception, but her lack of conviction is revealed in this line—she is torn between her moral principles and the social embarrassment of her situation.
c18:p24: Amy has just arrived at her mother's house with her child and belongings after separating from her husband Edwin Reardon, who has taken a low-paying clerk position and expects her to live in poverty. Mrs. Yule and Amy have been discussing in the entryway how to explain this separation to society, with Mrs. Yule suggesting they claim Reardon is mentally unstable. Mrs. Yule now invites Amy upstairs to the drawing-room to continue their conversation in a more comfortable setting.
c18:p25: This passage describes Mrs. Yule's physical appearance and demeanor as Amy arrives at her mother's house after separating from her husband Edwin Reardon. c18:p26: Amy has just arrived unexpectedly at her mother's house with her child and belongings, having separated from her husband Edwin Reardon who has taken a clerk's position at low wages. Mrs. Yule was unprepared for Amy's arrival, having expected her the following day.
c18:p27: Mrs Yule's response when Amy unexpectedly arrives at her home with her child and belongings after separating from her husband Edwin Reardon, explaining that Amy's bedroom is not prepared since she wasn't expected until the next day.
c18:p28: Amy has unexpectedly arrived at her mother's house with her child and belongings after separating from her husband Edwin Reardon, who has taken a poorly-paid clerk position. Mrs. Yule, though concerned about social appearances, is preparing to accommodate her daughter in the household despite the practical difficulties this will create for her already overworked servants.
c18:p29: Mrs. Yule offers her own bedroom to her newly-arrived daughter Amy, who has unexpectedly returned home with her child and belongings after separating from her husband Edwin Reardon. Mrs. Yule then goes to prepare the household arrangements, revealing her capacity for sharp, authoritative management of servants despite her outward gentility.
c18:p30: Amy has just arrived unexpectedly at her mother Mrs. Yule's house, having separated from her husband Edwin Reardon. Mrs. Yule offers Amy her own room, but upon checking on the household preparations, she discovers things are not ready. This passage captures the moment when Mrs. Yule's gentle, plaintive demeanor abruptly transforms into harsh severity as she addresses a servant, revealing how financial anxiety drives her to treat working-class employees with callous cruelty—a stark contrast to her affectionate kindness toward family members.
c18:p31: Amy has just arrived at her mother's house with her child and belongings after separating from her husband Edwin Reardon, who has taken a low-paying clerk position rather than continue his novel-writing career. Mrs. Yule has suggested that Amy claim Reardon is mentally unstable to explain the separation to society. Amy is now alone, troubled by the rumor her mother wants to spread, when this moment of reflection occurs.
c18:p32: Amy has just arrived at her mother's house with her child and belongings, having left her husband Edwin Reardon. Mrs. Yule questions Amy about Reardon's refusal to proceed with an earlier arrangement, apparently regarding his employment plans or financial strategy.
c18:p33: Mrs Yule and Amy discuss Edwin Reardon's refusal to continue with his original plan to earn money through novel-writing, instead taking a clerk position at twenty-five shillings a week, which Amy must now explain to her mother.
c18:p34: Mrs. Yule expresses bewilderment at Edwin Reardon's refusal to continue with his original plan to earn money, interpreting his decision to take low-wage clerk work instead as irrational behavior that suggests possible mental illness.
c18:p35: Amy defends her husband Edwin Reardon's decision to take low-wage clerical work instead of continuing novel-writing, though she acknowledges it reflects weakness and selfishness rather than mental illness as her mother suggests.
c18:p36: Amy speaks harshly about her husband Edwin Reardon's failure as a novelist, claiming he chooses easy work over the hard work of writing, even though she knows this characterization is unfair to his actual situation.
c18:p37: Mrs. Yule reacts with shock and disbelief to Amy's revelation that her husband Edwin Reardon has taken a clerk position earning only twenty-five shillings a week and expects his family to live on this meager wage. Mrs. Yule suggests Reardon must be mentally unbalanced or deliberately trying to abandon Amy, as she cannot fathom how an educated man of his station could expect his wife to accept such degrading poverty.
c18:p38: Amy denies her mother's suggestion that Edwin Reardon's refusal to continue with his original plan indicates mental disturbance, insisting instead that his behavior stems from weakness and selfishness in accepting low-wage clerical work rather than pursuing his novel-writing career.
c18:p39: Mrs Yule is questioning Amy about her husband Edwin Reardon's expectation that she live with him on minimal wages (twenty-five shillings a week) while he works as a clerk. Amy has recently returned to her mother's house after separating from Reardon, and Mrs Yule is attempting to understand how Reardon could possibly believe such poverty-level circumstances would be acceptable for his educated wife and child.
c18:p40: Mrs. Yule expresses disdain for her son-in-law Edwin Reardon's proposal that Amy live on twenty-five shillings a week, using the word "wages" scornfully to describe his clerk's income as beneath their social standing.
c18:p41: Amy defends her husband Reardon's financial plan to her mother, explaining that while he seeks work as a clerk for twenty-five shillings a week, he also expects to earn fifty pounds a year through writing, which would bring their total annual income to approximately one hundred pounds—a sum Mrs. Yule considers impossibly inadequate for supporting a family.
c18:p42: Mrs. Yule is responding to Amy's mention that her husband Edwin Reardon has taken low-paying clerical work at twenty-five shillings a week and hopes to earn additional money through anonymous writing. Mrs. Yule expresses her shock at his proposal for them to live on such meager wages, suggesting his behavior indicates either mental illness or deliberate abandonment of his wife.
c18:p43: Mrs. Yule suggests that Edwin Reardon has either gone mad or deliberately abandoned Amy by asking her to live on impossibly low wages (twenty-five shillings a week). c18:p44: Amy defends her husband Edwin Reardon against her mother's suggestion that he is mentally unbalanced. She explains that Reardon has simply failed as a novelist—his writing ability has declined, his last book was rejected, and he has accepted his financial ruin and expectation of poverty. Amy clarifies that his request for her to live on modest working-class wages stems from his realistic assessment of their circumstances, not madness or deliberate cruelty.
c18:p45: Mrs. Yule expresses her distress over Amy's separation from her husband Edwin Reardon and the social embarrassment it creates. She laments that if Reardon had simply gone to Worthing for the summer, they could have maintained appearances and avoided gossip. Now that Amy has returned home with her child and belongings, Mrs. Yule struggles with how to explain the situation to their social circle, as her entire life revolves around managing others' opinions and preserving respectability.
c18:p46: This passage occurs after Amy has returned to her mother's house following her separation from her husband Edwin Reardon, who has taken a clerk position at low wages. Mrs Yule is preoccupied with how to explain Amy's sudden return to their social circle while maintaining appearances. c34:p100: Alfred Yule learns that his daughter Marian's marriage to Jasper Milvain has been indefinitely postponed. c34:p101: Marian has just informed her father Alfred Yule that her marriage to Jasper is being indefinitely postponed. When he asks why, she gives a vague answer. c34:p102: Marian tells her father that the fifteen hundred pounds from her legacy will be invested for the benefit of herself, her parents, and her mother, offering to support them financially while maintaining her engagement to Jasper, whose career ambitions require him to remain unmarried for several years.

c34:p104: Marian has just inherited nearly fifteen hundred pounds and offers to use this money to support her father Alfred Yule and her mother while postponing her marriage to Jasper Milvain. c34:p105: Marian has just received news of her inheritance of fifteen hundred pounds. Marian interrupts his objection, offering to lend him the money as she would a stranger, with repayment possible once his eyesight is restored through the planned operation.
c34:p106: Marian offers her inherited money to support her parents, framing it as a loan to preserve her father's dignity. c34:p107: Marian offers to lend her inheritance money to her father Alfred Yule to support the family while he recovers from his eye disease. Yule responds with reservedness, saying he needs time to consider the offer.
c34:p108: Marian asks her father if he would like her to invite her mother to join them in his study, offering to end their private conversation about financial matters and her postponed marriage to Jasper.
c34:p109: Marian asks her father Alfred Yule if she should invite her mother to sit in his study room, and he consents to this arrangement after Marian has offered to lend him her legacy money to support the family while her eyes recover from his illness.
c34:p110: After Marian receives her inheritance of fifteen hundred pounds, she decides to use it to support her parents rather than marry Jasper immediately. This sentence marks the resolution of their financial discussion, with Alfred accepting her proposal without further objection.

c34:p112: Dora questions Jasper's decision to postpone his marriage to Marian indefinitely, challenging whether he is comfortable allowing Marian to financially support herself, her parents, and eventually him through her literary work while he pursues career advancement.
c34:p113: Jasper defends his decision to postpone marriage to Marian, saying he cannot help the circumstances that force the delay, when his sister Dora criticizes him for allowing Marian to toil to support her parents while remaining engaged to him.
c34:p114: Dora criticizes her brother Jasper for postponing his marriage to Marian indefinitely, insisting he should marry her within a year given that Marian will be supporting her parents with her modest inheritance and earnings.

c34:p116: Dora Milvain confronts her brother Jasper about his decision to postpone marriage to Marian indefinitely. c34:p119: Whelpdale, after achieving success with his newly transformed weekly publication Chit-Chat, encounters Jasper Milvain on the Strand in an unusually excited and disheveled state, having apparently received news that will dramatically alter his fortunes and social position.
c34:p120: Whelpdale encounters Jasper on the Strand in a state of excitement to announce that he has secured a position as editor of the transformed weekly paper Chit-Chat at two hundred fifty pounds per year, following a quarrel between the previous editor and another staff member.
c34:p121: Jasper encounters Whelpdale on the Strand in an unusually excited state. Whelpdale has just been offered a position as editor on the successful new publication Chit-Chat at two hundred and fifty pounds a year, which he announces with manic enthusiasm.

c34:p128: Jasper encounters Whelpdale on the Strand after Whelpdale's success with the Chit-Chat publication. c34:p130: Jasper agrees to attend a dinner that Whelpdale is organizing to celebrate his new position earning two hundred and fifty pounds a year at the journal Chit-Chat.
c34:p131: After Whelpdale secures a lucrative position as editor on the newly successful *Chit-Chat* publication and hosts a dinner celebrating his good fortune, Jasper and Dora embark on a three-week holiday to the Channel Islands, where they encounter evidence of the magazine's widespread circulation and receive letters from Whelpdale that will have significant romantic consequences for Dora.

c34:p133: Jasper and Dora are on holiday in the Channel Islands. c34:p134: Jasper and Dora are on holiday in the Channel Islands. After seeing a copy of Chit-Chat newspaper on Sark, Jasper writes to Whelpdale to inform him of the paper's success even there. This sentence introduces Whelpdale's reply to that letter.
c34:p135: Jasper and Dora are staying in the Channel Islands on holiday. Jasper questions the propriety of Whelpdale writing to her at all, but Dora responds that Whelpdale writes to her as respectfully as he does to Jasper. c34:p137: Jasper and Dora are on holiday in the Channel Islands. They receive letters from Whelpdale, and when Dora gets hers, she takes it upstairs to read privately, suggesting she is hiding something about Whelpdale's romantic intentions toward her from her brother.
c34:p138: Jasper and Dora are on holiday in the Channel Islands when they receive letters from Whelpdale. Dora receives a letter proposing marriage, which she encourages. c34:p139: Dora receives a letter from Whelpdale while on holiday in the Channel Islands with her brother Jasper. When Jasper asks what Whelpdale wrote to her, she responds with this line, deflecting from revealing that Whelpdale has proposed marriage to her in his letter.

c34:p141: Jasper reads aloud a letter from Whelpdale while on holiday in Sark with his sister Dora. c34:p142: Jasper has received a letter from Whelpdale while on holiday in Sark with his sister Dora. c34:p143: Dora reacts with delight to Jasper's witty observation about Whelpdale's reverence for him increasing the better they know each other, while they are on holiday in the Channel Islands. c34:p144: Jasper and Dora have received letters from Whelpdale while on holiday in Sark. c34:p145: Jasper asks his sister Dora to show him a letter she received from Whelpdale while they were on holiday in Sark. c34:p146: Jasper asks to see a letter that Whelpdale sent to Dora while they were on holiday in the Channel Islands. Dora deflects his request by claiming she left it upstairs, refusing to show him the letter in which Whelpdale has proposed marriage to her.
c34:p147: Jasper expresses disapproval of Whelpdale writing to Dora while they are on holiday in the Channel Islands, viewing it as presumptuous behavior that overstepped social boundaries based on their difference in social position.
c34:p148: Dora defends Whelpdale's respectful correspondence with her to Jasper, hinting at a developing romantic relationship between them that Jasper has not yet discovered.

c34:p150: Jasper and Dora are on holiday in the Channel Islands. After receiving letters from Whelpdale, Jasper jokingly suggests that Whelpdale is being presumptuous in writing to them at all. c34:p151: Dora defends Whelpdale's social standing to her brother Jasper, who has dismissed Whelpdale as beneath their class after learning of Whelpdale's proposal to her.

c34:p153: Dora defends Whelpdale's social position to Jasper during their holiday in the Channel Islands, arguing that despite his lower status as a journalist, his financial success with Chit-Chat makes him economically superior to both siblings.
c34:p154: Dora sarcastically dismisses Jasper's concern about money when he criticizes Whelpdale's position as inferior, asserting that Whelpdale actually earns more income than they do. c34:p155: Dora laughs at her brother Jasper's dismissive comment about Whelpdale's position and income, responding that money is what matters despite Jasper's claim that he writes "for honour and glory."
c34:p156: Dora sarcastically responds to Jasper's dismissal of Whelpdale's financial success, mocking his pretension that literary work is about honor and glory rather than money, especially since Whelpdale now earns more than they do.
c34:p157: Jasper and Dora are on holiday in the Channel Islands after Maud's wedding. While reading letters from Whelpdale on Sark, Dora reveals that he has proposed marriage to her. c34:p158: Dora reveals to her brother Jasper that Whelpdale has proposed marriage to her while they are on holiday in Sark. This moment marks a turning point in the narrative, as it sets in motion events that will complicate Jasper's own romantic entanglements and commitments.
c34:p159: Jasper's shocked reaction when Dora tells him that Whelpdale has proposed marriage to her while they are on holiday in Sark.
c34:p160: Dora's response when Jasper calls Whelpdale's marriage proposal to her "astounding impudence," questioning whether he truly means it.
c34:p161: Jasper's disapproving reaction to his sister Dora's revelation that Mr. Whelpdale has proposed marriage to her. c34:p162: Dora responds to her brother Jasper's objection to Mr. Whelpdale's marriage proposal. Despite Jasper calling Whelpdale's proposal "astounding impudence," Dora decides to reject him civilly, and Jasper then directs her to do so while maintaining their friendly relations with him.
c34:p163: Dora responds with surprise and confirmation when Jasper instructs her to refuse Whelpdale's marriage proposal. c34:p164: Jasper advises his sister Dora on how to respond to Whelpdale's marriage proposal, instructing her to reject him politely while maintaining their friendship and keeping the proposal secret from Jasper himself.
c34:p165: Dora questions whether Jasper is serious when he instructs her to refuse Whelpdale's marriage proposal while maintaining their friendship, during their holiday in the Channel Islands.
c34:p166: Jasper Milvain instructs his sister Dora to reject Whelpdale's marriage proposal politely while maintaining their friendship, asserting his authority over her response and demanding her obedience in the matter.

c34:p169: Jasper expresses his ambitions to Dora after visiting their sister Maud's luxurious new home following her marriage to Mr. Dolomore. c34:p170: Dora responds affirmatively to Jasper's statement that he aims at "something higher" than Maud's fashionable but superficial life in high society, affirming her own ambitions for greater literary and intellectual achievement.
c34:p171: Jasper expresses concern to his sister Dora about her apparent friendliness toward Whelpdale, a man who has recently proposed to her and is now financially successful after the triumph of the Chit-Chat publication.

c34:p173: Jasper expresses suspicion about Dora's interactions with Whelpdale, suggesting the man should be unhappy given his rejected proposal to her, but noting he appeared cheerful instead—part of their conversation after Dora's visit to their newly married sister Maud.
c34:p174: Dora defends her cordial behavior toward Whelpdale by attributing his good mood to the success of his new publication Chit-Chat, during a conversation with Jasper about Whelpdale's proposal of marriage to her.

c34:p176: Dora confronts Jasper after learning rumors that he has been acting as if he is no longer engaged to Marian Yule, despite their ongoing engagement. She demands to know the truth about whether he has been representing himself as free.
c34:p177: Dora confronts Jasper about rumors that he has been representing himself as no longer engaged to Marian, asking him to deny the gossip she has heard from Maud about Mrs. Betterton and Mrs. Lane.
c34:p178: Dora confronts Jasper about rumors that he is no longer engaged to Marian, demanding he deny the false gossip that has circulated through Mrs. Lane's social circle.

c34:p180: Jasper denies to his sister Dora that he has spread rumors about ending his engagement to Marian, dismissing gossip that has circulated through society about his supposed freedom from the engagement.
c34:p181: Dora confronts Jasper about rumors that he is no longer engaged to Marian. When Jasper dismisses the gossip, Dora reveals her source: Maud heard it from Mrs Betterton, who learned it from Mrs Lane, a society figure connected to their circle.
c34:p182: Jasper has been secretly proposing to Miss Rupert while still engaged to Marian. c34:p183: Dora confronts Jasper about rumors that he is no longer engaged to Marian, demanding he confirm or deny the claim. This question comes after Maud has reported that Mrs. Betterton heard from Mrs. Lane that Jasper has been representing himself as free from his engagement.

c34:p198: Jasper confesses to his sister Dora that he has proposed to Miss Rupert while still engaged to Marian, and is waiting for Miss Rupert's response from Germany, acknowledging the unpleasant nature of his betrayal.

c34:p200: Jasper confesses to his sister Dora that he has proposed to Miss Rupert while still engaged to Marian Yule. c34:p201: Dora confronts Jasper after learning he has proposed to Miss Rupert while still engaged to Marian. She questions the morality of his betrayal, asking what his disloyal behavior should be called.
c34:p202: Jasper defends his behavior to his sister Dora after confessing that he has proposed to Miss Rupert despite being engaged to Marian. He is arguing that his betrayal of Marian was inevitable given the circumstances.
c34:p203: Dora confronts Jasper after learning he has proposed to Miss Rupert while still engaged to Marian. She expresses her moral disapproval of his betrayal, questioning whether he truly understands the shamelessness and cruelty of abandoning Marian at her moment of greatest need.
c34:p204: Jasper confesses to Dora that he proposed to Miss Rupert while still engaged to Marian, claiming he was tempted by Miss Rupert's intellect and wealth during a dinner at the Ruperts' house.
c34:p205: Dora confronts Jasper about his proposal to Miss Rupert while he is still engaged to Marian. c34:p206: Jasper confesses to his sister Dora that he has proposed to Miss Rupert, a wealthy and intellectual woman, while still engaged to Marian. He admits he yielded to temptation despite knowing this betrayal is wrong, and waits for Miss Rupert's response to his proposal.
c34:p207: Dora confronts Jasper after learning he has proposed to Miss Rupert while still engaged to Marian. She expresses moral outrage at his betrayal of Marian, who is financially supporting her struggling parents.

c34:p213: Jasper confesses to his sister Dora that he has proposed to the wealthy Miss Rupert while still engaged to Marian, betraying his commitment. c7:p147: Mrs Yule mentions to Alfred that Marian received a letter from the Miss Milvains, which prompts a discussion about their brother Jasper Milvain and whether he should be invited to visit the Yule household.

c7:p149: Mrs Yule is speaking to her husband Alfred about Marian receiving a letter from the Miss Milvains. c7:p151: Mrs. Yule is speaking to her husband Alfred about their daughter Marian's disappointment that he did not invite Jasper Milvain, a young man Marian met in the country, to visit their London home. c7:p153: Alfred Yule is defending his decision not to invite Jasper Milvain to visit their London home. c7:p154: Alfred Yule is having a rare moment of good humor after receiving praise in Mr. Hinks's book. c7:p155: Mrs Yule urges her husband Alfred to reconsider his dismissal of young Jasper Milvain, suggesting that their daughter Marian's loneliness and marriageable age warrant allowing him to visit, despite Alfred's reservations about the young man's prospects and character.
c7:p156: Alfred Yule's wife mentions that Marian never meets young men and suggests it isn't right for her at her age. Alfred agrees with this observation before pausing to reflect on the matter of Jasper Milvain potentially visiting their home.
c7:p157: Alfred Yule, after learning from his wife that their daughter Marian may be disappointed he hasn't invited Jasper Milvain to visit, reflects on whether he should encourage the young man's interest in his daughter, weighing his concerns about Milvain's prospects and his own need for Marian's assistance with his work.
c7:p158: Mrs Yule expresses concern to her husband Alfred about their daughter Marian's isolation, suggesting he should encourage the young man Jasper Milvain to visit their home, as Marian appears to have romantic interest in him based on a letter she received from his sisters.
c7:p159: Alfred Yule discusses his concerns about Jasper Milvain with his wife, questioning whether the young man should be encouraged to visit Marian. c7:p160: Alfred Yule is discussing with his wife whether Jasper Milvain should be invited to visit their daughter Marian. Yule expresses reservations about Milvain's prospects and character, doubting whether the young man has a secure future or is merely flirting with Marian.
c7:p161: This passage occurs during Alfred Yule's private contemplation in his study, after his wife has just broached the subject of Jasper Milvain's potential interest in visiting Marian. c7:p163: Alfred Yule reflects on whether becoming editor of The Study would reduce his dependence on his daughter Marian's assistance, and considers that Jasper Milvain might have potential, as his wife has gently suggested Marian may be interested in the young man.
c7:p164: Alfred Yule is defending his decision not to invite Jasper Milvain to visit, after his wife suggests that Marian is disappointed by his absence. c7:p165: Mrs Yule responds to her husband Alfred's question about whether she knows if Jasper Milvain has any wish to visit Marian, after she had suggested that their daughter seems disappointed that Milvain hasn't been invited to their home.
c7:p166: Alfred Yule questions his wife about her assumption that their daughter Marian is interested in Jasper Milvain, after Mrs. Yule suggests that Marian was disappointed her father didn't invite the young man to visit them in London.
c7:p167: Mrs Yule is speaking to her husband Alfred about their daughter Marian's apparent interest in Jasper Milvain, a young man Marian met in the country. c7:p168: Alfred Yule discusses with his wife his reservations about Jasper Milvain's intentions toward their daughter Marian, who has been receiving letters from Milvain's sisters and appears to harbor romantic feelings for him.
c7:p169: Alfred Yule expresses doubt about Jasper Milvain's character and intentions toward his daughter Marian, suggesting the young man may be untrustworthy and that it would be better if he did not visit. c7:p170: Mrs. Yule expresses alarm when Alfred Yule suggests that Jasper Milvain may be untrustworthy and merely seeking to amuse himself with their daughter Marian, urging her husband to prevent him from visiting their home.
c7:p171: Alfred Yule is discussing his reservations about Jasper Milvain with his wife, who has suggested that Marian is disappointed Yule hasn't invited Milvain to visit. c7:p172: Alfred Yule decides against encouraging Jasper Milvain's visits to his daughter Marian, fearing the young man is unreliable. Mrs. Yule accepts this decision reluctantly, acknowledging that it is probably best to prevent any romantic connection.
c7:p173: Alfred Yule advises his wife not to mention Jasper Milvain to their daughter Marian, after discussing whether they should encourage the young man's visits. c7:p174: Mrs. Yule agrees not to mention Jasper Milvain to her daughter Marian, after Alfred Yule expresses his disapproval of the young man and advises his wife to keep silent about him.
c7:p175: Mrs. Yule hesitates to leave her husband's study after discussing Jasper Milvain with him. c7:p176: Alfred Yule's wife, Mrs. Yule, is expressing concern to her husband that the Milvain sisters' continued correspondence with Marian may lead to frequent mentions of their brother Jasper, whom Alfred disapproves of as a potential suitor for his daughter. c7:p177: Alfred Yule and his wife discuss whether Jasper Milvain should visit their home. Mrs. Yule worries that if the Milvain sisters continue corresponding with Marian, they will mention their brother, which Yule finds unfortunate since he disapproves of Milvain as a suitor for his daughter.
c7:p178: Mrs. Yule suggests to her husband Alfred that Jasper Milvain may have encouraged his sisters to write to Marian, implying he has romantic intentions toward their daughter.
c7:p179: Alfred Yule, after learning from his wife that Marian may be interested in Jasper Milvain, makes a somewhat dismissive comment about women's subtlety while reflecting on whether Milvain might have asked his sisters to write to Marian as a way to maintain contact.
c7:p180: Alfred Yule makes a subtle remark about women's subtlety regarding Jasper Milvain, and his wife Mrs Yule fails to grasp his meaning, displaying her characteristic struggle to understand intellectual concepts due to her limited education.
c7:p181: Alfred Yule is discussing Jasper Milvain with his wife, who suggests that Milvain may have serious intentions toward their daughter Marian. c7:p182: Mrs Yule expresses concern to her husband Alfred about their daughter Marian's isolation and limited social opportunities, particularly regarding her inability to meet suitable young men like Jasper Milvain.
c7:p183: Alfred Yule dismisses his wife's concerns about their daughter Marian's loneliness, insisting that her life devoted to literary work is satisfactory, though he acknowledges things may improve if he obtains the editorship of The Study.

c7:p190: Mrs. Yule returns to her sewing after a conversation with her husband Alfred about whether he should invite Jasper Milvain to their home, sensing that their daughter Marian has romantic feelings for him. c7:p191: Mrs. Yule reflects on her conversation with her husband Alfred about their daughter Marian's lack of social opportunities and potential interest in Jasper Milvain. c7:p192: Mrs. Yule reflects on her decision not to accompany her husband and daughter to visit John Yule's house, recognizing that her lower-class origins and lack of education are a source of shame to her husband Alfred and a social liability that constrains Marian's freedom and prospects, particularly regarding potential suitors like Jasper Milvain.
c7:p193: Mrs Yule reflects on her inadequacy as an educated woman and fears that her lower-class background would repel Jasper Milvain if he were to visit, thus preventing any romantic connection between him and her daughter Marian.

c7:p196: Mrs Yule, sitting late into the night sewing while her husband works in his study, admits to her husband Alfred that she has forgotten the time. c7:p197: At the end of the evening, Alfred Yule corrects his wife's grammar as she sits late with her sewing, reminding her not to revert to poor speech habits—a final illustration of the social distance and tension that defines their marriage and affects their daughter Marian's prospects.
c8:p0: This opening passage introduces Alfred Yule's circle of old acquaintances from his earlier years—specifically three couples representing "men with unpresentable wives" whose marriages have hindered their professional advancement in the literary world. The detailed portraits of Hinks, Gorbutt, and Christopherson establish a recurring theme in the chapter: how men of talent and ambition have been thwarted by their choice of wives from lower social classes, setting up the broader narrative about Yule's own disappointments and his judgment of others' life choices.
c8:p1: This chunk appears in paragraph P1, immediately following Alfred Yule's observations about his acquaintances—Hinks, the Gorbutts, and the Christophersons—whose literary careers have been hindered by their marriages to women of lower social status. The narrator's commentary suggests that these men's failures stemmed not from lack of talent but from their choice of wives, implying that prudent marriages to women of equal social standing would have enabled their success.
c8:p2: This chunk introduces Mr Quarmby as one of Alfred Yule's old acquaintances who has remained unmarried and views married men with scorn. It appears in a section cataloguing several of Yule's friends whose wives are considered socially unsuitable, contrasting Quarmby's bachelor status with the domestic failures of men like Hinks, Gorbutt, and Christopherson. Quarmby later becomes a gossip who spreads rumors about Yule's potential editorship of The Study.
c8:p3: This chunk describes Alfred Yule's social behavior with his circle of old literary acquaintances—men with unsuccessful careers and unpresentable wives. It establishes Yule's pattern of seeking intellectual authority and validation through gatherings at his house, where they collectively mock and criticize prominent literary figures, followed by his inevitable physical and emotional decline afterward. This characterizes Yule's desperate need for social esteem despite his failed career aspirations.
c8:p4: **Context:** After Alfred Yule's disappointment at losing the editorship position of The Study to a younger, unknown scholar, this chunk describes how a rumor—spread by the chatty Mr. Quarmby—initially raised Yule's hopes by suggesting he would get the job. Though Yule enjoyed the sudden attention and congratulations from acquaintances and old friends, his doubts grew as weeks passed without hearing from Mr. Rackett himself, ultimately presaging his eventual rejection.
c8:p5: Alfred Yule had been rumored to be appointed editor of the literary journal *The Study* following Fadge's departure. This passage reveals that despite the widespread gossip spread by Mr. Quarmby and the congratulations from Yule's acquaintances, the proprietor Mr. Rackett ultimately chose a different candidate—a young, scholarly provincial sub-editor with no connections to London's literary world. This disappointment deeply affects Yule, triggering weeks of sullen misery that impacts his entire household, and becomes a turning point that influences subsequent events in the narrative.
c8:p6: Alfred Yule's disappointment after losing the editorship of The Study to a younger, provincial candidate. Despite harboring secret doubts about his own prospects, Yule reacts with anger when confronted by Quarmby about the failed appointment, then retreats into brooding silence at home with his family.
c8:p7: This chunk appears in paragraph P7 and reflects Alfred Yule's internal rationalization of why he was passed over for the editor position at The Study magazine. After the announcement that a younger provincial scholar would get the job instead of him (P5), Yule attempts to convince himself he wasn't disappointed by dwelling on his lack of wealth, social connections, and advancing age—disadvantages that make it difficult for established literary figures to advance in the competitive publishing world. The chunk acknowledges that proprietor Rackett had briefly considered Yule as a foil to the outgoing editor Fadge, but ultimately rejected him on the advice of others.
c8:p8: Alfred Yule has been passed over for the editorship of The Study magazine, a position he believed he might obtain. Despite his initial announcement of this disappointment with apparent indifference, the rejection deeply affects him, plunging the household into gloom. During this difficult month, Yule becomes withdrawn and irritable with his wife and daughter. When Marian offers him a gesture of affection one evening, he unexpectedly opens up to her about his failures and the obstacles he believes have hindered his literary career, particularly his inability to move in the right social circles and his disadvantageous marriage.
c8:p9: Alfred Yule's bitter monologue to his daughter Marian following his disappointment at not being offered the editorship of The Study. He blames his failure on poverty and lack of social connections, contrasting himself with Fadge, whose advantageous marriage enabled his career success. Yule expresses resentment that his modest circumstances prevented him from cultivating the social relationships necessary for professional advancement in literary journalism.
c8:p10: After Alfred Yule's disappointment at not securing the editorship of *The Study*, he becomes withdrawn and bitter. One evening, when Marian offers him an affectionate gesture, he unexpectedly unbburdens himself to her about his failures, blaming his lack of social connections and his wife's lowly origins for his inability to advance in the literary world. Marian is troubled by his harsh implicit accusations against her mother and cannot respond, leading him to abruptly dismiss her with "Good-night."
c8:p11: This passage occurs after Marian's father, Alfred Yule, has been disappointed in his hopes to become editor of The Study. Following a brief moment of emotional connection with her father, during which he bitterly recounts the obstacles poverty has placed in his path to literary success, Marian retreats to her room in despair. The chunk captures her private anguish over her own constrained life as an unpaid literary drudge, her unfulfilled romantic hopes for Jasper Milvain from their time together at Finden, and her sense that she bears an equal burden of suffering from the family's financial circumstances, though her father only acknowledges his own disappointments.
c8:p12: This passage occurs after Marian has experienced profound despair and loneliness following her disappointment about Jasper Milvain and her father Alfred's bitter reaction to being passed over for the editorship of *The Study*. Isolated and emotionally exhausted from her literary work at the British Museum, Marian reflects on her inability to confide her true feelings to Dora and Maud Milvain, despite their friendly correspondence, as she must maintain a façade of contentment in her letters to them.
c8:p13: After Alfred Yule's disappointment at not being offered the editorship of The Study, he becomes withdrawn and bitter at home. His wife had previously begun to hint to him about the possibility of Marian forming a connection with Jasper Milvain, but now abandons these attempts. This chunk marks the point where Mrs Yule gives up trying to facilitate any relationship between her daughter and Milvain, deciding instead to let matters proceed as they have been, maintaining the status quo of silence and inaction regarding the young man.
c8:p14: Marian searches the British Museum Reading Room for Jasper Milvain during November, hoping to encounter him again after their acquaintance has seemingly ended due to her father's disapproval and Jasper's association with the rival magazine editor Fadge. Her visits to the Museum become a place where she both works and secretly seeks glimpses of him, reflecting her emotional distress over their separation.
c8:p15: This passage occurs in late November as Marian Yule sits in the British Museum Reading Room, experiencing despair and existential doubt about her work as a literary hack. It follows her father Alfred's disappointment at being passed over for the editorship of *The Study* and his bitter recriminations to her about his failed career. Marian's profound discouragement reflects both her own trapped circumstances as a poorly paid copywriter and her loneliness after the abrupt cessation of her brief acquaintance with Jasper Milvain.
c8:p16: Marian, exhausted and despondent while studying at the British Museum Reading Room, reflects critically on the futility of literary work and her own situation. She questions the value of writing mere literary criticism and commercial hack work when she has no genuine message to convey, contrasting this with her father Alfred Yule, who similarly produces only secondary critical writing rather than original creative work.
c8:p17: This passage occurs during Marian Yule's moment of profound despair while working alone in the British Museum Reading Room on a gloomy November afternoon. Exhausted by her hack literary work and questioning the purpose of her life, she contemplates the futility of the endless cycle of literary production and her own entrapment in it. This represents the emotional nadir of her circumstances before her chance encounter with Jasper Milvain moments later.
c8:p18: This passage occurs during Marian Yule's moment of profound despair and disillusionment in the British Museum Reading Room. Exhausted from literary hackwork and questioning the value of her labor, she fantasizes about manual work and sardonically imagines an automaton that could replace writers like herself by mechanically combining existing books into new ones for contemporary consumption. The passage reflects her growing depression over her trapped circumstances—intellectual work without genuine purpose, poverty, and thwarted personal happiness following her separation from Jasper Milvain.
c8:p19: Marian is sitting alone in the British Museum Reading Room, deeply discouraged about her meaningless work as a literary hack. As the fog outside grows thicker and the electric lights flicker on, she experiences a moment of profound despair, imaginatively transforming the physical space around her into a hellish prison where she and her fellow researchers are trapped souls.
c8:p20: Marian sits exhausted in the British Museum Reading Room on a gloomy November afternoon, unable to concentrate on her work. Overwhelmed by despair about her life of literary drudgery and longing for Jasper Milvain, she struggles with the poor electric lighting as she attempts to force herself to focus on her reading task before ultimately deciding to abandon her work and go home to cry.
c8:p21: Marian has been working at the British Museum Reading Room, deeply discouraged about her life of literary drudgery. After months of avoiding Jasper Milvain following his involvement with the rival magazine The Current, she unexpectedly encounters him as she returns books, marking a crucial turning point in their relationship.
c8:p22: Marian encounters Jasper Milvain unexpectedly at the British Museum library after months of separation. Upon seeing her, Jasper's face brightens with genuine pleasure, suggesting his delight at their chance meeting.
c8:p23: Jasper Milvain encounters Marian Yule in the British Museum's Reading Room after months of separation. He greets her warmly and offers to help her carry books, initiating their first conversation since their acquaintance was interrupted by her father's disapproval of Jasper's association with the editor Fadge.
c8:p24: Marian encounters Jasper Milvain at the British Museum after months of avoiding him. When he asks how she likes the weather and electric lighting, she dismissively replies "It's very bad," referring to both the foggy conditions and harsh artificial light that make reading impossible.
c8:p25: Jasper Milvain encounters Marian at the British Museum library after months of separation. He greets her warmly as she is leaving, commenting on the fog and poor electric lighting before asking if she is departing.
c8:p26: Marian confirms she was going alone to leave the British Museum when Jasper Milvain offers to accompany her home through the fog.

c9:p0: Edwin Reardon begins writing his new book with disciplined effort, calculating that he can complete a three-hundred-page volume in forty-five days by writing four manuscript slips daily. c9:p1: Edwin Reardon, a struggling novelist, calculates that completing his manuscript will take forty-five days. He hopes to sell the book by Christmas for approximately seventy-five pounds, which would allow him to pay his rent and gain a few weeks of mental rest. c9:p2: This passage depicts Reardon's psychological torment during his sleepless nights as he struggles to write a three-volume novel under financial pressure. c9:p3: Edwin Reardon, struggling to complete a novel while facing financial desperation and mental exhaustion, has calculated he can finish his book in forty-five days for a mere seventy-five pounds. c9:p5: Edwin Reardon, a struggling novelist facing financial desperation and marital strain, contemplates suicide as a solution to his poverty and perceived inability to provide for his wife Amy and son Willie. c9:p6: Edwin Reardon struggles with the psychological burden of writing a three-volume novel under financial pressure. c9:p7: Edwin Reardon abandons Milvain's advice to write a sensational novel and instead commits to a story in his natural style—a thin narrative difficult to expand into three volumes. c9:p8: Edwin Reardon, a struggling novelist, has established a rigorous daily writing schedule to complete a three-volume book within forty-five days, hoping to earn enough money to pay rent and gain mental rest. c9:p9: Edwin Reardon struggles with creative paralysis while attempting to write a three-volume novel under financial pressure. c9:p10: This passage describes Edwin Reardon's mental deterioration as he struggles with writer's block while attempting to complete his three-volume novel under financial pressure. c9:p13: Edwin Reardon struggles with the declining quality of his writing as he works under severe time and financial pressure to complete a three-volume novel.
